text: In a eukaryotic cell, where are the protein complexes of the electron transport chain of aerobic respiration located?
solution: The electron transport chain is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (the cristae). It pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space; the matrix is where the Krebs cycle runs, and the cytoplasm is where glycolysis runs.

text: Yeast growing without oxygen carries out alcoholic fermentation. Which molecule does this pathway regenerate so that glycolysis can keep running?
solution: Glycolysis reduces \(\mathrm{NAD^+}\) to NADH. Without oxygen there is no electron transport chain to reoxidise it, so fermentation does it instead: acetaldehyde is reduced to ethanol and \(\mathrm{NAD^+}\) is released for glycolysis to use again.

text: ATP synthase makes most of the ATP in a respiring cell. Where does the energy it uses come directly from?
options: The hydrolysis of GTP made in the Krebs cycle
The transfer of a phosphate group from glucose
The splitting of water inside the matrix
The flow of protons down their gradient across a membrane
The breakdown of pyruvate to carbon dioxide
solution: The electron transport chain pumps protons across the inner membrane. ATP synthase lets them flow back down their electrochemical gradient and uses that energy to join ADP and phosphate (chemiosmosis). Transfer of a phosphate from a substrate is substrate-level phosphorylation, which makes far less ATP.

text: A plant is supplied with water made with the heavy oxygen isotope \(^{18}\mathrm{O}\) and carbon dioxide with ordinary oxygen. Where does the \(^{18}\mathrm{O}\) appear first?
options: In the glucose made by the Calvin cycle
In the oxygen gas released by the plant
In the RuBP that fixes carbon dioxide
In the NADPH made in the thylakoids
It stays in the water and is never used
solution: The light-dependent reactions split water (photolysis) to replace electrons lost by photosystem II, releasing its oxygen as \(\mathrm{O_2}\). So the labelled oxygen leaves as oxygen gas. The oxygen atoms in glucose come from carbon dioxide.

text: A pancreatic cell makes a digestive enzyme for export. Which organelle modifies the enzyme and packs it into vesicles that travel to the cell membrane?
solution: Ribosomes on the rough ER make the protein, which moves to the Golgi apparatus. The Golgi modifies it (for example by adding sugars) and buds it off in secretory vesicles, which fuse with the cell membrane (exocytosis).

text: Red blood cells are placed in a salt solution that is more concentrated than their cytoplasm. What happens to them?
options: They lose water by osmosis and shrink
They swell and burst, because water enters by osmosis
They take in salt by active transport until they burst
They swell but do not burst, because the cell wall resists
Nothing, because the membrane is impermeable to water
solution: The solution is hypertonic, so water moves out of the cells by osmosis, from the higher water potential inside to the lower one outside. The cells shrink and look crinkled. Red blood cells have no cell wall, which is why in pure water they would burst instead.

text: Which blood vessel carries oxygen-rich blood from the lungs back to the heart?
solution: The pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. They are the only veins in the adult that carry oxygen-rich blood; the pulmonary artery is the only artery carrying oxygen-poor blood.

text: In a healthy kidney, glucose filtered out of the blood is almost all taken back. In which part of the nephron does this happen?
solution: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs all the glucose and amino acids and most of the water and salts, using cells with microvilli and many mitochondria for active transport. Bowman's capsule is where filtration happens, not reabsorption.

text: The template strand of a short stretch of DNA reads 3'-TACGGA-5'. What is the mRNA transcribed from it?
solution: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template, with U in place of T. Pairing T-A, A-U, C-G, G-C, G-C, A-U gives AUGCCU, running 5' to 3' because the template runs 3' to 5'. 5'-UCCGUA-3' is the same bases read the wrong way round.

text: How many different three-base codons can be made from the four bases found in mRNA?
solution: Each of the three positions can hold any of 4 bases, so there are \(4^3 = 64\) codons. 61 of them code for amino acids and 3 are stop codons; 20 is the number of amino acids they code for.

text: Two parents are both carriers of the recessive allele for cystic fibrosis. What is the probability that their next child is a carrier who does not have the condition?
solution: Cross Ff x Ff: the children are FF : Ff : ff in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1. Carriers who are not affected are Ff, so the probability is 2/4 = 1/2. The value 2/3 answers a different question: the chance that a child already known to be unaffected is a carrier.

text: Which statement correctly describes a competitive inhibitor of an enzyme?
options: It binds to a site away from the active site and changes the enzyme's shape permanently
It increases the maximum rate the enzyme can reach
It binds to the active site, and its effect can be overcome by adding more substrate
It always forms covalent bonds with the enzyme
It lowers the activation energy of the reaction
solution: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site. Raising the substrate concentration makes the substrate win more often, so the maximum rate is unchanged. Binding away from the active site describes a non-competitive inhibitor.

text: A solution has a pH of 4. What change in the hydrogen ion concentration brings its pH to 6?
solution: pH is \(-\log_{10}[\mathrm{H^+}]\), so each unit of pH is a factor of 10. Going from pH 4 to pH 6 means \([\mathrm{H^+}]\) falls from \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-6}\) mol/L, a decrease of \(10^2 = 100\) times.

text: What is the conjugate base of the dihydrogen phosphate ion, \(\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}\)?
solution: A conjugate base is what remains after the acid loses one proton. \(\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-}\) minus \(\mathrm{H^+}\) is \(\mathrm{HPO_4^{2-}}\). \(\mathrm{H_3PO_4}\) is its conjugate acid, and \(\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}\) is two protons away.

text: Which of these compounds is a structural isomer of butan-1-ol?
solution: Isomers share a molecular formula. Butan-1-ol is \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}\), and so is ethoxyethane, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OC_2H_5}\). Butanal is \(\mathrm{C_4H_8O}\), butanoic acid \(\mathrm{C_4H_8O_2}\), propan-1-ol \(\mathrm{C_3H_8O}\) and butane \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\).

text: Ethene decolourises bromine water at room temperature. What type of reaction is this?
solution: Bromine adds across the C=C double bond, giving a saturated product (1,2-dibromoethane, or a bromo-alcohol in water). Nothing is replaced and nothing is lost, so it is an addition reaction, the typical reaction of alkenes.

text: A strip of zinc is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution: \(\mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu}\). Which species is the oxidising agent?
solution: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) gains two electrons and is reduced to Cu, so it is the oxidising agent: it oxidises zinc. Zinc loses electrons and is the reducing agent. Sulfate is a spectator ion.

chapter: States of Matter and Gas Laws
text: A sample of an ideal gas occupies 6.0 L at 300 K. The pressure is kept constant while the gas is heated to 450 K. What is its new volume?
solution: At constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature (Charles's law): \(V_2 = V_1 \times T_2/T_1 = 6.0 \times 450/300 = 9.0\) L. Using Celsius temperatures, or inverting the ratio (4.0 L), are the usual slips.

text: Which of these molecules is linear?
solution: In \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) the carbon has two double bonds and no lone pairs, so the two electron regions sit at 180°. \(\mathrm{H_2S}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) are bent because of lone pairs on the central atom, \(\mathrm{PH_3}\) is pyramidal and \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\) tetrahedral.

text: The synthesis of ammonia, \(\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3}\), is exothermic. What happens to the equilibrium when the temperature is raised at constant pressure?
options: It shifts to the right, increasing the yield of ammonia
It does not move; only the rate increases
It shifts to the left, decreasing the yield of ammonia
It shifts to the right, because molecules collide more often
solution: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, here the reverse reaction, so the equilibrium shifts left and the yield of ammonia falls. For an exothermic reaction the equilibrium constant also falls as temperature rises.
